title: Treating Non-infectious Disease: Immunotherapy for Melanoma
subtitle: How checkpoint inhibitors work, what the survival data show, and where treatment is heading
subject: Biology
syllabusModule: Module 8 Non-infectious Disease and Disorders (2017) + Biotechnology (2025)

lessonIntent: Students can explain how checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy treats advanced melanoma, analyse trial data to evaluate it, and discuss current and future applications of biotechnology for melanoma.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, treating melanoma with immunotherapy. Let's get into it.

scenes.caption: Treating Non-infectious Disease: Immunotherapy for Melanoma

scenes.heading: Releasing the brakes on the immune system
scenes.body: Some melanoma drugs don't attack the tumour at all. They take the brakes off the patient's own immune system.
scenes.callout: How does a molecular mechanism turn into a survival statistic?
scenes.caption: Checkpoint inhibitors release immune brakes, turning a Nobel Prize idea into longer survival for melanoma.

voiceover.text: Australia has one of the highest melanoma rates in the world, and for a long time, once melanoma had spread through the body, most patients died within about a year. Chemotherapy barely helped. Then came a strange idea. Instead of attacking the cancer directly, what if you took the brakes off the immune system and let it do the job? Cancer cells often switch off the T cells that should kill them, by pressing on molecular brakes called C T L A four and P D one. James Allison and Tasuku Honjo showed that blocking those brakes with a drug lets the T cells wake up and attack the tumour, and in twenty eighteen they shared the Nobel Prize for it. Today we'll follow that one biotechnology all the way, how it works, what the data say, and where it's heading next.

scenes.heading: Melanoma: treatment depends on the stage
scenes.body: Melanoma is a cancer of the pigment cells in the skin. How it is treated and managed depends on how far it has spread.

bullets.text: Early melanoma: surgery removes it, and that is often curative.
Advanced melanoma: drugs are needed, because it has spread beyond the skin.
About half of melanomas carry a BRAF mutation, which targeted drugs can block.
Management: regular skin checks and sun protection to catch or prevent new melanomas.

scenes.callout: Once melanoma spreads, surgery alone is not enough.
scenes.caption: Early melanoma is cut out; advanced melanoma needs targeted drugs or immunotherapy.
scenes.recapSeed: Early melanoma is removed by surgery; advanced melanoma needs drug therapy.

voiceover.text: First, the disease. Melanoma is a cancer of melanocytes, the pigment cells in the skin, and it's strongly linked to UV exposure. How it's treated depends on how far it has spread. When it's caught early and still in the skin, surgery to cut it out is often enough to cure it. But once it has spread to lymph nodes or other organs, surgery alone can't reach it all, so drugs are needed. About half of melanomas carry a mutation in a gene called B R A F, and for those patients, targeted drugs can block the faulty protein. Immunotherapy works for melanomas with or without that mutation. And alongside any treatment, management means regular skin checks and sun protection, to catch new melanomas early or stop them forming. Today we're focusing on the biotechnology that changed advanced melanoma most, checkpoint inhibitors.

scenes.heading: The words you need
scenes.body: Five terms describe how this treatment works and how we measure it.

bullets.text: Immune checkpoint: a receptor that switches a T cell off, stopping attacks on healthy tissue.
Checkpoint inhibitor: a drug that blocks a checkpoint so T cells stay active.
Monoclonal antibody: many identical antibodies, made in the lab to bind one target.
Overall survival: the percentage of patients still alive after a set time.
Adverse event: a harmful side effect that occurs during treatment.

scenes.callout: Checkpoints are brakes; checkpoint inhibitors block the brakes.
scenes.caption: Immune checkpoint, checkpoint inhibitor, monoclonal antibody, overall survival, adverse event.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down five terms. An immune checkpoint is a receptor that switches a T cell off, a built in brake that stops the immune system attacking healthy tissue. A checkpoint inhibitor is a drug that blocks one of those checkpoints, so the T cells stay active. These drugs are monoclonal antibodies, many identical antibodies made in the lab, all designed to bind one specific target, and that's what makes this a biotechnology. Then two terms for reading the data. Overall survival is the percentage of patients still alive after a set time, like five years. And an adverse event is a harmful side effect that happens during treatment. Keep those last two in mind, because evaluating any treatment means weighing survival against side effects.

scenes.heading: How checkpoint inhibitors work
scenes.question: Explain how a PD-1 inhibitor such as nivolumab or pembrolizumab treats melanoma. Cover the normal job of the PD-1 pathway, how cancer exploits it, and how the drug disrupts that.
scenes.coachNote: Build it as a chain: normal function, then the cancer's trick, then the drug's block, then the outcome.
steps: Normally, when PD-L1 binds the PD-1 receptor on a T cell, it sends an off signal that calms the immune response and prevents autoimmunity.
Cancer cells exploit this by displaying lots of PD-L1, switching off the T cells that should kill them, so the tumour hides.
Pembrolizumab is an antibody that binds PD-1 and blocks the PD-L1 connection, so the off signal can't be sent.
The T cells stay active, recognise the cancer, and destroy it; immune memory can keep the response going.
Answer: the drug releases an immune brake the cancer was pressing, so the patient's own T cells clear the tumour ✓
scenes.caption: PD-1 inhibitors block the off signal cancer uses, so the patient's T cells attack the tumour.

voiceover.text: Let's walk through the mechanism the way an extended response should, as a chain. First, the normal function. The P D one receptor sits on T cells, and when a molecule called P D L one binds it, it sends an off signal that calms the T cell down. That's a useful brake, because it stops the immune system attacking healthy tissue. Second, the cancer's trick. Many tumour cells cover themselves in P D L one, so they press that brake on any T cell that comes near, and the cancer escapes attack. Third, the drug. A P D one inhibitor, like nivolumab or pembrolizumab, is a monoclonal antibody that binds the P D one receptor and blocks P D L one from connecting, so the off signal can't be delivered. Fourth, the outcome. The T cells stay switched on, recognise the cancer as abnormal, and kill it, and because the immune system forms memory, the response can last for years. So the drug releases a brake the cancer was exploiting. It restores an immune response, rather than generally boosting immunity.

scenes.heading: Analysing the data: five-year survival
scenes.body: A large randomised trial of 945 patients with advanced melanoma compared three immunotherapy options.

bullets.text: Ipilimumab alone (blocks CTLA-4): about 26% alive at five years.
Nivolumab alone (blocks PD-1): about 44% alive at five years.
Both drugs together: about 52% alive at five years.

scenes.secondary: Before checkpoint inhibitors, most patients with advanced melanoma died within about a year. Randomisation means the groups started out similar, so differences in survival can be linked to the treatment.
scenes.callout: Blocking both brakes gave the highest survival.
scenes.caption: Five-year survival: about 26% on ipilimumab, 44% on nivolumab, 52% on the combination.
scenes.recapSeed: Combination 52%, nivolumab 44%, ipilimumab 26% alive at five years.

voiceover.text: Now let's analyse the data, because that's how you actually evaluate a biotechnology. In a large randomised trial, nine hundred and forty five patients with advanced melanoma were split into three groups. One group got ipilimumab alone, which blocks C T L A four. Another got nivolumab alone, which blocks P D one. And the third got both together. After five years, about twenty six percent of the ipilimumab group were still alive, about forty four percent of the nivolumab group, and about fifty two percent of the combination group. Compare that with the era before these drugs, when most patients with advanced melanoma died within about a year. And because patients were randomly assigned, the groups started out similar, so the differences in survival can be linked to the treatment itself. Reading the chart, blocking both brakes gave the highest survival.

scenes.heading: Evaluating it: benefits and limitations
scenes.body: A strong evaluation weighs the survival gain against side effects, response rates and cost.

bullets.text: Benefit: long-lasting survival for many patients who once had months to live.
Limitation: freed T cells can attack healthy organs, causing colitis, hepatitis or thyroid damage.
Severe side effects hit more than half on the combination, about a quarter on nivolumab alone.
Not everyone responds, and the drugs are expensive, though subsidised in Australia.

scenes.secondary: The side effects follow directly from the mechanism: if you release the brakes, T cells can also attack healthy tissue, which is exactly what the checkpoint normally prevents.
scenes.callout: The mechanism explains both the benefit and the main risk.
scenes.caption: Checkpoint inhibitors extend survival, but can cause immune attacks on healthy organs.

voiceover.text: So how do we evaluate it. The benefit is huge, many patients who once had months to live are now alive years later, some with no sign of cancer. But there are real limitations. The first comes straight from the mechanism. If you take the brakes off T cells, they can also attack healthy organs, causing inflammation of the bowel, the liver or the thyroid gland. In that same trial, more than half of the patients on the combination had severe side effects, compared with about a quarter on nivolumab alone. So the combination gains some survival, at the cost of more harm. Second, not everyone responds, and even on the combination, nearly half of the patients in the trial had died by five years. And third, the drugs are very expensive, although in Australia they're subsidised for advanced melanoma. So a balanced evaluation says the survival benefit is strong, but it has to be weighed against toxicity for each patient.

scenes.heading: Future directions for melanoma treatment
scenes.body: Research is now asking when to give immunotherapy, and how to make it more personal.

bullets.text: Before surgery: giving immunotherapy first, while the tumour is still in place, can prime a stronger T cell response.
Personalised mRNA vaccines: built from each patient's tumour mutations, given with a PD-1 inhibitor.
Biomarkers: tests to predict who will respond, sparing others the side effects.

scenes.secondary: Australian researchers at Melanoma Institute Australia have helped lead this work. Georgina Long and Richard Scolyer were named joint Australians of the Year in 2024.
scenes.callout: The future is about timing and personalisation.
scenes.caption: Future directions: immunotherapy before surgery, personalised mRNA vaccines and response biomarkers.

voiceover.text: Finally, where is it heading. The first direction is timing. Researchers are giving immunotherapy before surgery, while the tumour is still in the body, so the T cells have plenty of cancer to learn from. In a large international trial, more patients stayed free of melanoma after a year with that approach than with the standard order. The second is personalisation. Personalised m R N A vaccines are built from the mutations in each patient's own tumour, to teach T cells exactly what to target, and they're given alongside a P D one inhibitor. Early trials showed fewer recurrences, and bigger trials are under way. And the third is biomarkers, tests that predict who will respond, so patients who won't benefit can be spared the side effects. Australian researchers have been central to this work, and melanoma specialists Georgina Long and Richard Scolyer were named joint Australians of the Year in twenty twenty four.

scenes.heading: Three traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: saying immunotherapy boosts the immune system. Checkpoint inhibitors release a specific brake, restoring a response the cancer had switched off.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: treating a survival percentage as a promise for one patient. Fifty-two percent alive at five years is a group result, not a personal guarantee. Trap 3: thinking immunotherapy is harmless because it uses the body's own defences. The same released T cells can attack healthy organs.
scenes.callout: Release, not boost; group data, not guarantees; natural is not harmless.
scenes.caption: Immunotherapy releases a brake; survival data describe groups; immune side effects are real.

voiceover.text: Three traps that cost marks. Trap one, saying immunotherapy boosts the immune system. Checkpoint inhibitors don't turn the whole immune system up. They block one specific brake, restoring a T cell response the cancer had switched off, and naming that brake is what earns the mark. Trap two, treating a survival percentage as a promise for one person. Fifty two percent alive at five years describes a group of patients in a trial, not a guarantee for any individual. Trap three, thinking immunotherapy must be harmless because it uses the body's own defences. The same released T cells that attack the cancer can also attack the bowel, the liver or the thyroid, which is why patients are monitored so closely. Release, not boost, group data, not guarantees, and natural is not the same as harmless.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: In the trial, five-year survival was about 52% on the combination and 44% on nivolumab alone. Severe side effects affected more than half on the combination and about a quarter on nivolumab. A student concludes the combination is always the better choice. Evaluate this claim.
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause and weigh survival against side effects.
answerSteps: The combination gave higher five-year survival, about 8 percentage points more.
But severe side effects were more than twice as common on the combination.
So the extra survival comes with more harm, and the best choice depends on the patient.
A frail patient might do better on nivolumab alone; a fit patient might accept the risk.
Answer: not always better; the combination trades higher survival for more toxicity.
scenes.caption: The combination gains survival but more than doubles severe side effects, so it is not always the better choice.

voiceover.text: Quick check, and this one is about reading data. In the trial, five year survival was about fifty two percent on the combination and forty four percent on nivolumab alone. Severe side effects affected more than half the patients on the combination, and about a quarter on nivolumab. A student concludes the combination is always the better choice. Evaluate that claim. Pause and weigh survival against side effects. Right. The combination did give higher survival, about eight percentage points more at five years. But severe side effects were more than twice as common. So the extra survival comes with extra harm, and the best choice depends on the patient. Someone frail might do better on nivolumab alone, while a fit patient might accept the higher risk for the extra benefit. So the claim is too absolute. The combination trades higher survival for more toxicity.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Early melanoma is removed by surgery; advanced melanoma needs drug therapy.
Checkpoint inhibitors are monoclonal antibodies that block CTLA-4 or PD-1 brakes on T cells.
Five-year survival: about 26% ipilimumab, 44% nivolumab, 52% combination.
Released T cells can attack healthy organs, so side effects must be weighed.
Future: immunotherapy before surgery, personalised mRNA vaccines, biomarkers.
scenes.finalPrompt: Evaluating a treatment? Explain the mechanism, read the survival and side-effect data, then give a conditional verdict.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: stage decides treatment, the mechanism, the data, the side effects, the future.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five things to take away. First, early melanoma is removed by surgery, but once it spreads, drug therapy is needed. Second, checkpoint inhibitors are monoclonal antibodies that block the C T L A four or P D one brakes on T cells, so the patient's own immune response attacks the tumour. Third, the data, about twenty six percent alive at five years on ipilimumab, forty four on nivolumab, and fifty two on the combination. Fourth, released T cells can attack healthy organs too, so survival always has to be weighed against side effects. And fifth, the future is about timing and personalisation, immunotherapy before surgery, personalised m R N A vaccines, and biomarkers. Whenever you evaluate a treatment, explain the mechanism, read the data, then give a conditional verdict. See you next lesson.
